title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 1
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each, with an explanation for every answer and your score by skill.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, and an explanation for every question.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. والنسبة اللي هتظهر في الآخر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 1
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes each. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest items, and Module 2 adapts to your Module 1 performance (it is harder or easier). In this practice test all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it.

questions.p: Ceramicist Nadia Fawzy spent months testing glazes made from desert sand before she found a mix that did not crack in the kiln. Her ______ approach—changing only one ingredient at a time and recording every result—allowed her to identify exactly which mineral was causing the cracks.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: impulsive
methodical
secretive
nostalgic
questions.e: Changing one ingredient at a time and recording every result describes a careful, step-by-step approach, so "methodical" fits. "Impulsive" is the opposite of that process, and "secretive" and "nostalgic" have no support in the text.

questions.p: Historians once described the medieval spice trade as a mainly European enterprise. Studies of merchant letters kept in Cairo and other Mediterranean cities have ______ that view, showing that Arab, Jewish, and Indian traders ran most of the routes across the Indian Ocean long before European ships arrived there.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: challenged
confirmed
inspired
simplified
questions.e: The letters show that non-European traders ran most routes, which goes against the older view, so the studies "challenged" it. "Confirmed" reverses the relationship; "inspired" and "simplified" do not describe evidence that contradicts a view.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of an older novel.
Mr. Hale was not a man given to ______. When the harvest failed, he spoke of it in the same even voice he used for the weather, and no neighbor ever heard him complain of his losses.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: economy
punctuality
lamentation
diligence
questions.e: The text stresses that Mr. Hale never complained, even after a failed harvest, so he was not given to "lamentation" (expressing grief or complaint). "Diligence" and "punctuality" are qualities the text never discusses, and saying he lacked "economy" (careful use of money) has no support.

questions.p: Although the committee's report was praised for its thoroughness, several economists found its conclusions ______: after two hundred pages of careful data, the authors recommended only that "further study may be useful," a suggestion so cautious that it gave lawmakers almost no direction.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: inflammatory
noncommittal
premature
redundant
questions.e: A recommendation so cautious that it gives "almost no direction" avoids taking a clear position: it is "noncommittal." "Inflammatory" (provoking anger) is the opposite of cautious; "premature" and "redundant" do not describe a lack of direction.

questions.p: For decades, astronomers assumed that the rings of Saturn formed at about the same time as the planet itself, roughly 4.5 billion years ago. Data from the Cassini spacecraft complicated that picture. The rings turned out to be remarkably clean: they are made almost entirely of bright water ice, with little of the dark dust that should have built up on them over billions of years. Some researchers now argue that the rings may be only a few hundred million years old.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It describes a scientific method and then explains why that method failed.
It compares the findings of two spacecraft and evaluates which is more reliable.
It presents a long-held assumption, describes evidence that raised doubts about it, and then mentions an alternative view.
It introduces a theory and then provides evidence that strongly confirms it.
questions.e: The text moves from an old assumption (rings as old as Saturn) to evidence against it (clean ice) to a new view (young rings). The "strongly confirms" choice reverses this, since the evidence raises doubts; only one spacecraft is mentioned, and no method "fails."

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story.
Amira had rehearsed her request on the tram, on the stairs, and at the very door of her uncle's office. __Yet when he looked up from his papers and asked, kindly enough, what she wanted, every sentence she had prepared seemed to fly out of the open window.__ She stood silent, turning her gloves over in her hands.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why the uncle is unwilling to listen to the character.
It suggests that the character has changed her mind about what she wants.
It shows that the character's careful preparation fails her at the moment she needs it.
It describes the place where the character practiced her request.
questions.e: After long rehearsal, Amira forgets everything when the moment comes, and the next sentence shows her standing silent. The uncle asks "kindly enough," so he is not unwilling to listen; nothing shows that she has changed her mind.

questions.p:
Text 1
Many nutrition guides advise students to eat breakfast to improve concentration at school. In a study by researcher Omar Haddad, students who ate breakfast scored higher on morning memory tasks than students who skipped it. Haddad concludes that breakfast directly improves students' ability to focus.

Text 2
Psychologist Rana Saleh notes that students who regularly eat breakfast also tend to sleep more and to follow steadier daily routines than those who skip it. Unless studies measure these habits, she argues, they cannot tell whether breakfast itself or the routines that come with it explain the higher scores.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Saleh (Text 2) most likely respond to Haddad's conclusion (Text 1)?
c: She would agree that breakfast directly improves focus, since the students who ate breakfast scored higher.
She would argue that the higher scores might be explained by other habits linked to eating breakfast, so his conclusion goes beyond his evidence.
She would question whether the students in his study really ate breakfast.
She would claim that sleep is more important than breakfast for success on memory tasks.
questions.e: Saleh says that, without measuring sleep and routines, a study cannot show that breakfast itself causes higher scores, so she would say Haddad's cause-and-effect claim is not proven. Claiming that sleep matters more is too strong: she only says the cause is uncertain.

questions.p: Economist Laila Hamdy studied small bakeries in three cities that began taking orders through a shared online service. Before joining, most of the bakeries threw away 15 to 20 percent of their bread each day. After a year of using the service, which let customers order the day before, waste fell to under 5 percent because the bakeries could bake much closer to the amount customers actually wanted. Hamdy notes that the savings were several times larger than the service's fees.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Hamdy found that bakeries in large cities waste more bread than bakeries in small towns.
Hamdy argues that online ordering services charge fees that are too high for most small bakeries.
Hamdy found that an advance ordering service helped bakeries cut waste by matching production more closely to demand.
Hamdy found that customers prefer ordering bread online to buying it in a shop.
questions.e: The text is about waste falling because bakeries could bake closer to what customers wanted. The fees choice is the opposite of the text (savings were several times the fees); cities and towns are never compared, and customer preferences are not discussed.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story. Selim is an old fisherman.
Every morning, before the sky had properly lightened, Selim walked to the end of the harbor wall and studied the water. He could not have said what he was looking for. The younger men laughed at him and checked the weather on their phones, yet when Selim shook his head and turned for home, few of them put out to sea that day.
questions.q: According to the text, what is true about the younger fishermen?
c: They will not go fishing until Selim has checked the weather on his phone.
They join Selim on the harbor wall each morning to study the water.
They believe that Selim can explain exactly what he looks for in the water.
Although they make fun of Selim's habit, they often follow his judgment about whether to go out.
questions.e: The young men laugh at Selim, yet when he shakes his head, few of them go out, so they follow his judgment. It is the young men, not Selim, who use phones; the text says Selim "could not have said" what he looks for.

questions.p: A desert shrub studied by botanist Yara Kamal has very small leaves covered in a thick layer of wax. Some researchers have suggested that these leaves mainly protect the shrub from plant-eating animals, which find them hard to chew. Kamal hypothesizes instead that the small, waxy leaves are mainly an adaptation that reduces the loss of water in the dry desert air.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Kamal's hypothesis?
c: Plant-eating animals in the region avoid the shrub's leaves because they taste bitter.
Shrubs of the same species growing in wetter valleys nearby have larger leaves with thinner wax, even where plant-eating animals are just as common.
The shrub produces flowers only in years when rainfall is above average.
Several other desert plants also have small leaves.
questions.e: If leaves become larger and less waxy where water is easier to get, while animals stay equally common, leaf shape tracks water, not animals, which supports Kamal. Bitter taste is about animals and so fits the rival idea; flowering and "other plants" do not test her hypothesis.

questions.p: "The Clockmaker's Daughter" is an original poem. In the poem, the speaker suggests that her father cared more about his work than about his family.
questions.q: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
c: "His shop smelled of oil and brass and dust, / And sunlight crossed the counter in long bars."
"The town would set its watches by his bell, / And trust the hour he gave them to be true."
"He mended every clock in town on time, / But missed my birthday supper every year."
"I learned to read the hours from his hands / Before I learned to read the words in books."
questions.e: Only the first quotation sets his reliable work against his absence from his daughter's birthday every year. The shop and the town's trust describe his work but say nothing about his family; learning the hours "from his hands" suggests closeness, not neglect.

questions.p:
Visitors to four museums in a city, 2023 (thousands)
Museum | Weekday visitors | Weekend visitors
Science Hall | 120 | 210
Textile Museum | 45 | 40
Modern Art Gallery | 80 | 150
City History Museum | 60 | 95

A city report notes that most of the city's museums received more visitors on weekends than on weekdays in 2023, but that this pattern did not hold for every museum. For example, ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
c: the Science Hall had more weekend visitors than any other museum in the table.
the Textile Museum had 40,000 weekend visitors, fewer than any other museum in the table.
the Modern Art Gallery had more weekday visitors than weekend visitors.
the Science Hall had 210,000 weekend visitors and 120,000 weekday visitors, whereas the Textile Museum had more weekday visitors (45,000) than weekend visitors (40,000).
questions.e: The example must show both the usual pattern and an exception; only the first choice does (Science Hall follows the pattern, the Textile Museum does not). The other two true choices give only one museum's figure, and the Modern Art Gallery actually had more weekend visitors (150 vs 80).

questions.p:
Average daily screen time of teenagers in a survey (hours)
Age | Before 6 p.m. | After 6 p.m.
13 | 1.4 | 1.9
15 | 1.6 | 2.8
17 | 1.7 | 3.5

Researcher Hana Adel used a survey to study teenagers' use of phones, tablets, and computers. She concluded that as teenagers get older, the increase in their screen time happens mainly in the evening.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Adel's conclusion?
c: At every age in the table, teenagers spent more time on screens after 6 p.m. than before 6 p.m.
Seventeen-year-olds spent an average of 1.7 hours a day on screens before 6 p.m.
From age 13 to age 17, average screen time after 6 p.m. rose by 1.6 hours, while screen time before 6 p.m. rose by only 0.3 hours.
From age 13 to age 17, screen time before 6 p.m. rose more than screen time after 6 p.m.
questions.e: The conclusion is about where the increase happens, so you need the two increases: 3.5 − 1.9 = 1.6 hours after 6 p.m. against 1.7 − 1.4 = 0.3 before. "More time after 6 p.m. at every age" is true but says nothing about the change with age; the last choice reverses the data.

questions.p: Archaeologists excavating an ancient farmhouse in a river valley found storage jars containing wheat, barley, and dried dates. Chemical tests showed that the wheat and barley were grown in fields near the farmhouse, but the dates came from an oasis more than 250 kilometers away. Because carrying goods over such distances was costly at the time, the archaeologists suggest that the people living in the farmhouse ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: found it too costly to grow wheat and barley in the fields near their home.
grew their own dates in fields beside the farmhouse.
ate more dates than any other food.
were able to obtain goods through long-distance trade and could afford to pay for them.
questions.e: Costly goods from 250 km away suggest the household had access to trade and the means to pay for it. The grain was grown nearby, so it was not too costly to grow; the dates came from far away, not from fields beside the house; nothing compares amounts of food.

questions.p: The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on ______ some weather stations there have recorded almost no rain in their entire history.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Earth,
Earth
Earth;
Earth, and,
questions.e: Both parts are complete sentences, so a semicolon can join them. A comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and "and," with a comma after it wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

questions.p: Umm Kulthum, a singer whose monthly radio concerts were followed by listeners from Morocco to ______ remains one of the most celebrated performers in the history of Arabic music.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Iraq
Iraq;
Iraq—
Iraq,
questions.e: The phrase "a singer whose … Iraq" is extra information that opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "remains." A dash would not match the opening comma, and a semicolon cuts the subject off from its verb.

questions.p: Long before the region became a desert, rivers flowed across it. The researchers who mapped one ancient riverbed hidden beneath the desert ______ satellite radar images that can detect features buried several meters below the surface.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: sand, used
sand; used
sand: used
sand used
questions.e: The subject is "The researchers who mapped … sand," and its verb is "used." No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, so any comma, semicolon or colon here is wrong.

questions.p: After three years of tests, the museum's conservators settled on a single method for cleaning the old ceiling ______ a soft gel that lifts dirt away without dissolving the fragile paint underneath.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: paintings:
paintings;
paintings
paintings, it was
questions.e: A complete sentence comes before the blank, and what follows explains which method was chosen, so a colon is correct. A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, but "a soft gel …" is not one; "paintings, it was" makes a comma splice.

questions.p: The pattern of tiny, tooth-like scales covering a shark's skin ______ the drag the animal experiences as it swims. Engineers have studied this pattern in the hope of designing smoother, more efficient surfaces for ships.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: reduces
reduce
are reducing
have reduced
questions.e: The subject is the singular noun "pattern," not "scales" or "skin," so it needs the singular verb "reduces." "Reduce," "are reducing" and "have reduced" are all plural forms.

questions.p: Each spring, the city's community gardens hold a seed exchange. Gardeners bring seeds saved from ______ own plants and trade them for varieties they have not yet grown.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: their
they're
its
there
questions.e: The pronoun refers to "Gardeners" (plural) and shows possession, so "their" is correct. "They're" means "they are," "there" is a place word, and "its" is singular.

questions.p: Hoping to protect coral from rising sea temperatures, marine biologist Amal Darwish ______ heat-tolerant corals in an underwater nursery and then moved them onto damaged sections of the reef.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: raising
to raise
having raised
raised
questions.e: The sentence needs a main (finite) verb for the subject "Amal Darwish," and it must match the past tense of "moved." "Raising," "to raise" and "having raised" are not finite verbs, so they cannot be joined to the finite verb "moved" as the sentence's two main verbs.

questions.p: Most deserts are hot, but not all of them. The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and northern China, ______ has winters in which temperatures can fall below −30°C.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: however,
therefore,
in addition,
for example,
questions.e: The Gobi is an example of a desert that is not always hot, so "for example" fits. The contrast was already made by "but not all of them"; the Gobi sentence illustrates that point rather than contrasting with it, so "however" is wrong.

questions.p: Engineer Karim Salah designed a water filter made from clay and crushed rice husks. The filter can be made from materials that are easy to find in rural villages. ______ it can be produced by local workers using only simple tools.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Additionally,
Nevertheless,
For instance,
Conversely,
questions.e: The last sentence adds a second advantage to the first (easy materials, then simple tools), so "Additionally" is right. There is no contrast, which rules out "Nevertheless" and "Conversely," and the tools are not an example of the materials.

questions.p: In the early 1800s, most paper in Europe was made from cotton and linen rags, which were in limited supply. As demand for books and newspapers grew, paper makers searched for a cheaper and more plentiful raw material. ______ by the late 1800s, most paper was being made from wood pulp.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: Similarly,
Eventually,
In comparison,
For example,
questions.e: The text describes a search that, over time, led to a result, so a time word, "Eventually," fits. Nothing is being compared ("Similarly," "In comparison"), and wood pulp is the outcome of the search, not an example of it.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2024, engineer Mona Ezzat designed a solar-powered fishing boat for communities on Lake Manzala in Egypt.
• Traditional motorboats on the lake use diesel engines.
• Ezzat's boat uses solar panels on its roof to charge its battery.
• It can travel 40 kilometers on a single charge.
• Fishers who tested it said it was quieter and cheaper to run than diesel boats.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize an advantage of Ezzat's boat over traditional motorboats. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: According to fishers who tested it, Ezzat's solar-powered boat is quieter and cheaper to run than the diesel motorboats traditionally used on Lake Manzala.
Ezzat's boat, designed in 2024, uses solar panels on its roof to charge its battery.
Traditional motorboats on Lake Manzala are powered by diesel engines.
Ezzat's boat can travel 40 kilometers on a single charge.
questions.e: The goal asks for an advantage over traditional boats, so the sentence must compare the two; only the first does (quieter and cheaper). The other choices give true details about one boat only, with no comparison.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Psychologist Dina Rizk wanted to know whether background music affects how well students remember what they read.
• She asked 120 students to read the same article.
• Half read in silence; half read while instrumental music played.
• Afterward, all students answered 20 questions about the article.
• Students who read in silence answered an average of 15 questions correctly; those who read with music answered 12.
questions.q: The student wants to describe the method of Rizk's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Students who read in silence answered more questions correctly (15) than those who read with music (12).
Rizk wanted to find out whether background music affects how well students remember what they read.
Rizk had 120 students read the same article—half in silence, half with instrumental music playing—and then tested all of them with 20 questions about it.
Background music may make it harder for students to remember what they read.
questions.e: A method is what the researcher did: who took part, the two conditions and the test. Only the first choice describes this. The others give the results, the aim and a conclusion: true, but not the method.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform are two of the world's oldest writing systems.
• Hieroglyphs were often carved in stone or painted on walls and papyrus.
• Cuneiform was usually pressed into tablets of wet clay with a cut reed.
• Each system was in use for more than three thousand years.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the two writing systems. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Both Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform were in use for more than three thousand years.
Cuneiform was usually pressed into tablets of wet clay with a cut reed.
While Egyptian hieroglyphs were often carved in stone or painted on walls and papyrus, Mesopotamian cuneiform was usually pressed into wet clay with a cut reed.
Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform are two of the world's oldest writing systems.
questions.e: A difference needs both systems and a contrast word; only the "While …" sentence sets the materials of one against the other. The "Both …" choice gives a similarity, and the cuneiform-only choice mentions just one system.

questions.p: Ornithologist Teresa Lindqvist's account of the garden warbler's migration route is ______: rather than relying on a handful of sightings, it draws on location data from more than three hundred tagged birds tracked over five years.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: speculative
anecdotal
substantiated
provisional
questions.e: The colon explains why the account is strong: it rests on data from hundreds of birds over five years, so it is "substantiated" (supported by evidence). "Anecdotal" (based on a few stories) and "speculative" describe exactly what the text says the account avoids, and nothing suggests the account is only "provisional" (temporary).

questions.p: In her study of the first public museums in nineteenth-century Europe, historian Rania Gaber argues that curators did not merely respond to what visitors wanted to see. Instead, they actively ______ public taste, deciding which objects deserved display and arranging them in ways that taught visitors what to admire.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: molded
mirrored
recorded
disregarded
questions.e: Curators chose and arranged objects to teach visitors what to admire, so they "molded" (shaped) taste. "Mirrored" and "recorded" describe the passive role the text rejects ("did not merely respond"); "disregarded" contradicts the active influence described.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel.
Mrs. Ashworth received the news of her nephew's engagement with a composure so ______ that her companions, who had expected tears or at least a sharp remark, could not decide whether she was pleased, indifferent, or merely too proud to show her disappointment.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: theatrical
inscrutable
fragile
jubilant
questions.e: Her companions cannot tell what she feels, so her composure is "inscrutable" (impossible to read). "Theatrical" and "jubilant" would make her feelings obvious, and "fragile" suggests she is close to tears, the reaction the companions expected but did not see.

questions.p: The new climate model is more ______ than earlier versions—it divides the atmosphere into grid cells only a few kilometers wide instead of about a hundred—but its designers caution that finer detail does not automatically produce more accurate forecasts.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: volatile
granular
conventional
conservative
questions.e: The dashes explain the word: smaller grid cells mean finer detail, so the model is more "granular." "Volatile" (unstable) has no support, and "conventional" and "conservative" suggest sticking to old methods, the opposite of a new, more detailed model.

questions.p: Critics of philosopher Adel Lotfy charge that his essays ______ the hardest questions raised by his theory: instead of working through the strongest objections to his position, he typically mentions them in a single sentence and moves on.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
c: sidestep
resolve
anticipate
exaggerate
questions.e: Mentioning objections in one sentence and moving on avoids dealing with them, so the critics say he "sidesteps" them. "Resolve" is the opposite of what the critics claim. "Anticipate" is the strongest trap: it suggests he prepares answers to the objections, while the critics say he does not engage with them.

questions.p: Mapmakers face a problem that can never be fully solved: the Earth is round, but maps are flat. Every flat map of the world therefore distorts something, whether area, shape, distance, or direction. The Mercator projection, created in 1569, keeps the shapes of small areas accurate and was extremely useful to sailors, but it greatly enlarges regions far from the equator. On it, Greenland looks about as large as Africa, which is actually around fourteen times bigger.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that the Mercator projection should no longer be used.
To describe the history of mapmaking since 1569.
To explain that every flat world map involves a trade-off and to illustrate this with a well-known example.
To explain why sailors preferred maps that showed the true sizes of regions.
questions.e: The text states a general problem (all flat maps distort something) and then uses the Mercator map to show what is gained and what is lost. It never says to stop using the map (too strong), covers no wider history, and the Mercator map is the one that does NOT show true sizes.

questions.p: Many economists argue that cities should end rent controls because the controls discourage the building of new housing. Economist Farah Nassar accepts that strict controls can have this effect. __Her research, however, addresses a narrower question: what happens to long-time residents when controls are removed suddenly rather than gradually.__ In the two cities she studied, sudden removal was followed by a sharp rise in the number of residents leaving their neighborhoods, while gradual phase-outs produced much smaller changes.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It shifts the focus from a general debate to the specific issue that Nassar investigated.
It presents evidence against the claim that rent controls discourage construction.
It summarizes the results that Nassar found in the two cities.
It introduces a criticism of the methods Nassar used in her research.
questions.e: The sentence moves from the broad debate about rent controls to Nassar's narrower question, which the last sentence then answers. Nassar accepts the construction claim, so she does not argue against it, and the results come only in the following sentence.

questions.p:
Text 1
Linguists have often assumed that languages with many speakers change more slowly than small languages, because widespread use and written standards make new forms harder to spread. On this view, a language spoken by millions should resist change better than one spoken in a single village.

Text 2
Analyzing records of 80 languages over several centuries, linguist Kwame Asante found that the speed of vocabulary change was not related to the number of speakers. Languages changed fastest during periods of intense contact with other languages, such as conquest or expanding trade, whether they had a few hundred speakers or many millions.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Asante (Text 2) most likely respond to the assumption described in Text 1?
c: He would agree with it but add that it applies only to vocabulary.
He would argue that it misidentifies the factor that most affects how quickly a language changes.
He would argue that small languages actually change more slowly than large ones.
He would claim that written standards speed up change in languages with many speakers.
questions.e: Asante found that the number of speakers does not matter and that contact with other languages does, so Text 1 points to the wrong cause. Saying small languages change more slowly is a reversal: he found no link with size at all. He never discusses written standards.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story. Nour has returned to her family's village after many years in the city.
The lane was narrower than she remembered, and the baker's shop had become a stall that repaired phones. Yet the smell of the river was exactly the same, and when old Hajja Fatma called her by a childhood nickname that no one had used in twenty years, Nour found that she could not answer for a moment. She had prepared herself for the changes. It was what had stayed the same that undid her.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Nour is disappointed that the village has been modernized while she was away.
Nour has forgotten most of what the village looked like when she was a child.
Hajja Fatma is upset that Nour stayed away from the village for so long.
Nour is more deeply moved by what has stayed the same in the village than by what has changed.
questions.e: The last two sentences state the idea directly: she was ready for the changes, but the unchanged things "undid her." The disappointment choice reverses the focus, since the changes are what she had prepared for; she clearly remembers the village, and Hajja Fatma's feelings are not described.

questions.p: Marine biologist Sofia Arcuri studied a species of deep-sea shrimp that releases a cloud of glowing fluid when it is attacked. Earlier researchers had assumed that the sudden light simply startles predators into retreating. Arcuri's video recordings, however, show that predators often lunge at the glowing cloud itself while the shrimp escapes into the darkness. She suggests that the cloud works less like an alarm than like a decoy.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Arcuri found that the glowing fluid startles predators so much that they stop hunting.
Deep-sea shrimp produce light mainly in order to find food in the dark.
Video recordings are the most reliable way to study animals that live in the deep sea.
Arcuri's observations suggest that the shrimp's glowing fluid protects it mainly by drawing predators' attacks away from the shrimp itself.
questions.e: Arcuri's videos show predators attacking the cloud, not the shrimp, so the fluid acts as a decoy. The "startles predators" choice describes the earlier view that her work challenges; finding food and the reliability of video are never discussed.

questions.p: A small desert mouse studied by ecologist Rui Tanaka can live for months without drinking. Some researchers believe the mice survive by licking the dew that forms on rocks and plants in the early morning. Tanaka hypothesizes instead that the mice get nearly all the water they need from the dry seeds they eat, partly because their bodies produce water as they break down the food.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Tanaka's hypothesis?
c: The mice store seeds in underground burrows, where the air is more humid than at the surface.
The seeds eaten by the mice are also eaten by several species of desert birds.
The mice are active mainly in the hours after sunset, before any dew has formed.
In laboratory tests, mice given only the seeds they eat in the wild, with no other source of water, became dehydrated within a few days.
questions.e: If mice that eat only seeds quickly become dehydrated, seeds cannot supply nearly all their water, which directly weakens the hypothesis. Activity before dew forms would SUPPORT Tanaka (they cannot rely on dew), the humid burrows also fit his idea, and the birds are irrelevant.

questions.p:
Average score on a 50-point spatial reasoning test
Group | Before training | After 6 weeks
Video-game training | 31 | 38
Puzzle-book training | 30 | 35
No training | 31 | 32

Psychologist Imane Berrada assigned adults to three groups to test whether practice with a navigation video game improves spatial reasoning more than solving puzzle books does. She concluded that both kinds of training helped but that the video game was more effective.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Berrada's conclusion?
c: After six weeks, the video-game group had the highest average score of the three groups, at 38 points.
The video-game group's average score rose by 7 points and the puzzle-book group's by 5 points, while the score of the group with no training rose by only 1 point.
Before training, the puzzle-book group had a slightly lower average score than the other two groups.
The puzzle-book group's average score rose by 5 points, more than the video-game group's increase.
questions.e: The conclusion has two parts: both trainings helped (compared with no training) and the game helped more. Only the first choice shows both: +7 and +5 against +1. The "highest score" choice is true but does not show that puzzle books helped; the last choice is false (5 is less than 7).

questions.p:
Share of electricity generated by source in Country R (%)
Source | 2010 | 2015 | 2020
Coal | 52 | 41 | 27
Natural gas | 30 | 35 | 38
Wind and solar | 3 | 11 | 24
Other | 15 | 13 | 11

An energy analyst argues that the decline of coal in Country R was not mainly offset by natural gas, as is often assumed; instead, wind and solar grew to fill most of the gap. Specifically, ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the analyst's argument?
c: between 2010 and 2020, coal's share fell by 25 percentage points, while the share of natural gas rose by 8 points and that of wind and solar rose by 21 points.
in 2020, natural gas produced a larger share of Country R's electricity than any other source.
the share of electricity from wind and solar rose in every period shown, from 3 percent in 2010 to 24 percent in 2020.
coal's share fell from 52 percent in 2010 to 27 percent in 2020, while the share from other sources rose.
questions.e: The argument compares how much of coal's lost share went to gas and how much to wind and solar, so all three changes are needed: −25, +8 and +21. The wind-and-solar choice is true but gives no comparison with gas; the gas choice is true but supports the opposite emphasis; "other sources" actually fell (15 to 11).

questions.p: Historians studying a medieval trading city found that its oldest surviving tax records list dozens of goldsmiths but not a single glassmaker, even though glass objects from the same period have been found throughout the city. One explanation would be that all the city's glass was imported. Chemical analysis, however, shows that the glass was made with a type of sand found only in the city's own riverbed. This evidence suggests that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: glass was produced in the city even though the tax records do not list anyone who made it.
the tax records list the city's goldsmiths incorrectly.
glass objects were more valuable than gold objects in the city.
glassmakers in the city sent most of their products to other cities.
questions.e: Glass made from local sand must have been made locally, so glassmaking happened even though the records omit glassmakers. Nothing questions the goldsmith records, values are never compared, and exports are not mentioned (most glass was found in the city itself).

questions.p: Plants known as C4 plants, such as maize and many tropical grasses, photosynthesize especially efficiently in hot, bright conditions, while C3 plants, which include most trees and shrubs, do better in cooler or shadier conditions. The two groups leave different chemical traces, and the carbon in an animal's teeth reflects the plants it ate. Researcher Ines Moreau analyzed fossil teeth of grazing animals from one region and found that the proportion of C4 carbon in them rose steadily over two million years. This finding suggests that, over that period, ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: C4 plants became a larger part of the diet of the region's grazing animals.
the grazing animals in the region began to eat fewer plants overall.
maize was the main food of the region's grazing animals.
the region's grazing animals ate mainly trees and shrubs.
questions.e: Since tooth carbon reflects diet, more C4 carbon means the animals ate more C4 plants. The amount of food eaten is not measured; maize is only one example of a C4 plant, so that choice is too specific; and more C4 carbon points away from trees and shrubs, which are C3 plants.

questions.p: The festival's program featured three main events: a concert by the city's youth orchestra, which performed works by Egyptian composers; a talk by architect Hala Zaki, who described the restoration of several historic ______ and an exhibition of film posters from the 1950s.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: cinemas,
cinemas;
cinemas:
cinemas—
questions.e: SAT/ACT extra rule: when list items already contain commas, semicolons separate the items. The first item ends with a semicolon, so the second must too. A comma would blur the items together, and a colon or dash cannot separate list items.

questions.p: The wandering albatross—a seabird whose wings can stretch more than three meters from tip to ______ may spend several years at sea without once touching land.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: tip,
tip—
tip;
tip
questions.e: The extra information opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash before the verb "may spend." A comma does not match the opening dash, a semicolon separates the subject from its verb, and no punctuation leaves the dash pair unfinished.

questions.p: Cairo's metro, a key part of the city's transport system, opened its first line in ______ the network has grown to carry millions of passengers every day.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: 1987; since then,
1987, since then,
1987 since then,
1987, since then
questions.e: "Since then, the network has grown …" is a complete sentence, as is the first part, so a semicolon must separate them. A comma alone (with or without the comma after "then") makes a comma splice, and no punctuation makes a run-on.

questions.p: Researchers studying the tiny wasps that pollinate fig trees in the forests of southern ______ that each species of fig is usually pollinated by its own particular species of wasp.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: India, have found
India; have found
India have found
India—have found
questions.e: The long subject is "Researchers studying … southern India," and its verb is "have found." However long the subject is, no punctuation may separate it from its verb.

questions.p: The city library holds manuscripts from many centuries. Among the oldest objects in its collection ______ a set of astronomical tables that a scholar copied by hand in the fourteenth century.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: are
were
is
have been
questions.e: The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb, and it is "a set" (singular), not "objects." A singular subject needs "is"; the present tense also matches "holds." "Are," "were" and "have been" are all plural.

questions.p: Few novelists write about hospitals as convincingly as Yusuf Rahal does. Trained as a physician before he turned to fiction, ______ precise and unsentimental descriptions of illness and recovery.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the stories of novelist Yusuf Rahal are filled with
Yusuf Rahal's stories are full of
there are, in the stories of Yusuf Rahal,
the novelist Yusuf Rahal fills his stories with
questions.e: The opening phrase describes the person who trained as a physician, so the subject right after the comma must be Rahal himself. The other choices put "the stories" or "there" in that position, which creates a dangling modifier: the stories were not trained as physicians.

questions.p: Dating ancient art is notoriously difficult. The two competing research ______ findings, published in the same issue of the journal, reached opposite conclusions about the age of the cave paintings.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: team's
teams
teams's
teams'
questions.e: There are two teams (plural), and the findings belong to them, so the plural possessive "teams'" is correct. "Team's" is singular possessive, "teams" is plural but not possessive, and "teams's" is not a standard form.

questions.p: Some historians have described the scholars of Baghdad's House of Wisdom in the ninth century as mere translators of Greek texts. This view is incomplete. Scholars there did translate works by Greek writers such as Euclid and Ptolemy; ______ they also produced original work, as the mathematician al-Khwarizmi did when he wrote a book that laid the foundations of algebra.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: however,
therefore,
likewise,
for instance,
questions.e: The scholars did translate, but they also did original work: a contrast with the "mere translators" view, so "however" fits. "Therefore" wrongly makes original work a result of translating, and "likewise" and "for instance" do not signal the contrast.

questions.p: Most glass is made by melting sand at temperatures above 1,400°C, a process that uses large amounts of energy. A team led by materials scientist Kenji Oda has developed a way to produce glass at about 600°C using a liquid chemical mixture. For now, glass made this way is more expensive than ordinary glass. ______ the team expects the cost to fall as the process is scaled up for use in factories.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: As a result,
Even so,
In other words,
Similarly,
questions.e: The team expects costs to fall despite the current high price, so a contrast is needed: "Even so." "As a result" would mean the high price causes the fall, "In other words" signals a restatement, and "Similarly" signals a likeness.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek device recovered from a shipwreck in 1901.
• It was made more than two thousand years ago.
• It used interlocking bronze gears to predict the positions of the Sun and Moon and the timing of eclipses.
• No other known device with gears of similar complexity appears in the historical record for more than a thousand years afterward.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize how advanced the device was for its time. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Antikythera mechanism, an ancient Greek device, was recovered from a shipwreck in 1901.
The Antikythera mechanism used interlocking bronze gears to predict the positions of the Sun and Moon.
Recovered from a shipwreck in 1901, the Antikythera mechanism was made more than two thousand years ago.
More than two thousand years old, the Antikythera mechanism used bronze gears to predict eclipses, with a complexity not matched by any known device for more than a thousand years.
questions.e: "Advanced for its time" needs a comparison with what came after; only the first choice includes the fact that nothing similar is known for over a thousand years. The gears choice describes what it did but not how unusual that was for its age.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Air conditioners use large amounts of electricity.
• A wind catcher is a tall tower that catches breezes and directs them down into the rooms below.
• A courtyard lets hot air rise and escape, which draws cooler air into the surrounding rooms.
• Both methods have been used for centuries in hot regions such as Egypt and Iran.
• Neither method needs electricity.
questions.q: The student wants to present these cooling methods as an alternative to air conditioning. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Wind catchers and courtyards have been used for centuries in hot regions such as Egypt and Iran.
Instead of relying on electricity-hungry air conditioners, buildings can be cooled by wind catchers, which direct breezes into rooms, or by courtyards, which draw in cooler air as hot air escapes.
A wind catcher directs breezes down into rooms, while a courtyard lets hot air rise and escape.
A wind catcher is a tall tower that catches breezes and directs them down into the rooms below.
questions.e: Only the first choice sets the two methods against air conditioning ("Instead of relying on …"). The history choice and the "while" choice describe the methods without presenting them as an alternative, and the last choice describes only one method.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Astronomer Leila Okonkwo studies "rogue planets," planets that do not orbit any star.
• Rogue planets are hard to detect because they give off almost no light.
• Okonkwo uses a method called gravitational microlensing.
• The method detects how a planet's gravity briefly brightens the light of a more distant star behind it.
• In 2025, her team reported 12 new possible rogue planets.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce Okonkwo's research to an audience unfamiliar with rogue planets. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: In 2025, Okonkwo's team reported 12 new possible rogue planets found through gravitational microlensing.
Rogue planets give off almost no light, which makes them hard to detect.
Astronomer Leila Okonkwo studies rogue planets (planets that do not orbit any star) by detecting how their gravity briefly brightens the light of more distant stars.
Okonkwo uses gravitational microlensing to study rogue planets, which are hard to detect.
questions.e: An unfamiliar audience needs the term explained, and the research introduced: only the first choice defines rogue planets and says how Okonkwo studies them. The microlensing choices use the technical terms without explaining them, and the "no light" choice never mentions Okonkwo.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the explanation for EVERY question, including the ones you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason and not by luck.
For each mistake, write three things in your notebook: the skill tag, the trap that caught you (too broad, reversed, half-right, comma splice, and so on), and the rule or step you will use next time.
Look at your results by skill and list your two or three weakest skills.

Go back to the matching lessons: Words in Context; High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences; Sentence Boundaries; Commas and Extra Information; Colons, Dashes and Semicolons; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronouns; Verb Tense, Aspect and Finiteness; Modifiers, Parallel Structure and Comparisons; Plurals and Possessives; Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).
Redo the practice quiz on each of those lesson pages, then take Practice Test 2 under the same timed conditions.
